questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Anna Karenina and the motto the serial text omitted
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a first edition's motto shaped how the novel was read
questions.stem: A depot bulletin explains why the opening motto of a Russian novel about a wife's adultery was later dropped from the printed editions.

answer.exemplar: The motto, drawn from the Gospel of Matthew, tells the reader to take heed and listen, and it frames the whole book as a lesson rather than a picture of society. It appeared in the novel's first edition and was dropped from later printings, probably because a scriptural frame seemed too didactic and too religious for a work that argues its case through characters and plots.

questions.explanation: The motto addresses a reader who must take heed, and dropping it makes the novel look less like a lesson and more like a social portrait. Editorial choices change how a book presents itself.
questions.hint: Think about what the motto asks of its reader.

answer.exemplar: The author added a statement that he did not share the ideas implied by the epigraphs and by the closing section, which he had written under a religious influence he did not fully endorse. The disclaimer keeps the novel's argument open: a reader must weigh the text rather than take its front matter or its epilogue as the author's settled creed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Madame Bovary and the two editions fifty years apart
questions.learningObjective: Explain how censorship changed the genre of the novel
questions.stem: The depot's heritage panel explains why two printings of the same French novel can read very differently to a modern audience.

answer.exemplar: Because the first printing was cut by the publisher under pressure from the state prosecution, it lacks passages where the narrator's irony is sharpest and the narration itself is being mocked. A reader of that text sees a sombre story of adultery; a reader of the restored text sees a comic satire of provincial society and of the reader's own credulity, so the censorship changed the genre of the book.

questions.explanation: Cutting passages changes genre as well as length, since the irony is what makes the book a comedy of readerly credulity. How much of an author's tone is really an editor's decision?
questions.hint: Ask what the missing passages were doing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Anna Karenina and the motto the serial text omitted
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the removal of the motto changes in the reading experience
questions.stem: An annotation guide describes the removal of a biblical motto from later editions of a Russian novel and asks what the removal changes.

answer.exemplar: The removal withdraws an instruction to attend, so the book reads as observation rather than instruction, and readers who meet the restored motto later are meeting an argument about how the novel should be approached. Nothing happens to the characters or the plots; the whole difference lies in the posture the book takes towards the person reading it, which is why the motto belongs in a history of the text as much as in a history of the plot.

questions.explanation: A motto is an instruction to the reader, and without it the expectation of a lesson disappears. The characters and plots are untouched, so the difference lies in posture.
questions.hint: Ask what the motto instructed the reader to do.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate what the reader is expected to do with the dispute in the embedded scene
questions.stem: A discussion card asks what the reader is meant to do with the dispute between the church official and the young man once it ends.

options.text: To judge which of the two men has the better claim to be believed.
options.misconception: reads the ending as an invitation to take sides

options.text: To accept the old man's argument, since he has had years to test it.
options.misconception: assumes age and experience settle the argument

options.text: To decide for himself, since the novel declines to settle the dispute.
To leave the question aside, since it concerns the church alone.
options.misconception: thinks the dispute is a matter of institutional concern only

questions.explanation: The scene closes without a verdict, and the novel's larger structure does not answer in its place. The reader is left with a live question about freedom and comfort.
questions.hint: Ask whether anyone in the book settles it.
